items.title: Reflections on the Revolution in France
items.author: Edmund Burke
items.content: Written in 1790 during the early stages of the French Revolution, Reflections on the Revolution in France is regarded as one of the foundational texts of conservative political theory. In it, the British philosopher and statesman Edmund Burke critiques the political program of the French Revolution, dismissing it as a political order founded on abstract principles. Instead, Burke advocates for constitutional rule based on received institutions, incremental reform, and sensitivity to the vagaries of human nature. Some of Burke’s predictions, such as the revolutionary government becoming a “mischievous and ignoble oligarchy” and the politicization of the military bringing about a “military republic,” proved to be prescient in the face of the Reign of Terror and Napoleon’s coup of 18 Brumaire.

items.title: Short Fiction
items.author: Thomas Mann
items.content:
By the time Thomas Mann’s longer work finally established his fame, he had already been a published author of short fiction, primarily in the satirical magazine .

A typical Mann short story always has some element of psychological disquiet. Earlier in his career this often manifested in his stories as behaviors that caused the protagonists to endure ridicule (“Little Louise,” “The Path to the Cemetery”), but this evolved into entire characters who combine extra-societal behavior with a seeming inability to halt their descent into chaos (“Death in Venice,” “Mario and the Magician”). Woven through this are common themes: the secret world of children, the social mores of Wilhelmine Germany, and a love of dogs.

This collection includes many of Mann’s best known works. Particularly famous is “Death in Venice,” the candidly autobiographical story of a staid author’s obsession with a beautiful boy, which the included in its Great Books of the Western World set.

items.title: The Art of Illustration
items.author: C. H. Spurgeon
items.content: Though most well-known as the “Prince of Preachers,” C. H. Spurgeon was also the founder of and a lecturer at the Pastor’s College in London, later renamed “Spurgeon’s College” in his honor. is a posthumously published series of lectures given by Spurgeon late in his life to students at the college on the subject of improving their sermons through the use of metaphors, anecdotes, and other illustrations to strengthen the understanding and retention of the sermon by its listeners. Together, the lectures form a complete guide to the use of illustrations in preaching, from the introduction on how illustrations provide value, to demonstrating how to find or create illustrations, not only from mundane, everyday stories but also from the natural sciences. Being at the same time an academic, a voracious reader, and one of the most widely published Baptist preachers in history, Spurgeon brings a unique combination of expertise to the subject of illustration in public speech.

items.title: Within and Without
items.author: George MacDonald
items.content:
Brother Julian is far from an exemplary monk: he takes no joy in monastery life, feels no connection with God, and continuously dwells on the mysterious life he left behind. When he learns that a woman from his past needs his help, he must choose between his duty to the Church and his duty to his conscience.

George MacDonald’s earliest published work, and his only poetic drama, chronicles a monk’s journey to know God as he experiences love, death, and joy. Notably, it contains one of MacDonald’s earliest works of fantasy prose: a passage read by Julian from the fictitious book, .

items.title: The Final Count
items.author: H. C. McNeile
items.content:
Chemist Robin Gaunt believes he’s discovered the key to lasting world peace—in the form of the horrific poison gas he’s just perfected. Gaunt is certain that once the British government has the formula, no nation will ever dare start a war, for fear of the consequences. But Gaunt vanishes before can turn over the formula, and people start turning up dead—victims of some unknown poison.

It doesn’t take long for Bulldog Drummond to be on the case—and it doesn’t take long for him to realize that the man behind the kidnapping and murders is his arch enemy Carl Peterson. This leads to a final confrontation worthy of a Bond movie, as the hero and the evil genius face off in a giant zeppelin loaded with deadly toxin.

items.title: A Book-Lover’s Holidays in the Open
items.author: Theodore Roosevelt
items.content:
A Book-Lover’s Holidays in the Open is a travelogue written by former U.S. president Theodore Roosevelt about his expeditions through the Americas following his presidency in the early twentieth century. In it, Roosevelt takes readers on a cougar hunt in the Grand Canyon, through the Andes and Northern Patagonia, to a Mississippi River bird reserve, and to a Hopi snake dance, among other exotic and beautiful locations.

Roosevelt blends his love for reading and literature with these adventures, giving readers a glimpse into the books he would have brought on his outdoor journeys.

items.title: Brigadier Gerard Stories
items.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
items.content:
When Arthur Conan Doyle’s gallant French cavalryman Brigadier Gerard first appeared in print, the reading public was still reeling from the “death” of Conan Doyle’s most famous creation, Sherlock Holmes, the previous year. What they found in Brigadier Gerard was someone very different from the intense, emotionless consulting detective: a courageous and skilled, but vain and emotional, soldier-adventurer in search of glory for himself and for France, devoted to his elderly mother and the Emperor Napoleon in the extreme, and witness to some of the greatest events in European history as he fought the men and wooed the women of countless countries during the Napoleonic Wars. The Gerard of these stories is aged and retired, but vividly recounts the grand adventures of his youth, weaving romance and adventure, conflict and cunning, and world-changing events of military and political history with the human drama of those caught up in a turbulent era of war. His tales are thrilling ones in which he—of course—plays the leading role.

In writing the Brigadier’s tales of his adventures, Conan Doyle brought to bear his own knowledge of Napoleonic history, informed by the insights on warfare he gained in South Africa during the Boer War. His interest in sport is displayed in the tales which touch upon boxing, fox-hunting, and cricket. His keen eye as a social observer is evident in a number of stories where the Brigadier’s misperceptions of English society, prejudices from his own French viewpoint, and errors from his limited perspective of some events, highlight the idiosyncrasies of English life in both the upper and lower classes during the late Georgian and Regency eras.

In the dozen and a half stories collected here, readers will experience the Napoleonic Era from a perspective very unlike that of or other Napoleonic memoirs, histories, or works of fiction.

items.title: The Trap
items.author: Dorothy M. Richardson
items.content:
Series protagonist Miriam Henderson impulsively takes a flat in Flaxman Court with the very prim Selina Holland. Miriam struggles to introduce a disapproving Miss Holland to her bohemian London. Their apartment is across the way from that of a famous poet, E. W. Sayce—and Miss Holland is not impressed. (In later editions, Sayce is instead identified by Richardson as W. B. Yeats.)

As is typical in the Pilgrimage volumes, this is a story in which nothing much “happens”—Richardson herself dismissed the notion of plot as “lollipops for children”—but which paints a vivid and intimate portrait of a young writer’s mind, and brings to life the world that shaped her.

items.title: Malleus Maleficarum
items.author: Heinrich Kramer
items.content:
, often translated as , is a treatise on witchcraft by Heinrich Kramer published in 1486. At that time, witchcraft was not widely believed to be real, and prosecutions were rare. Many churchmen considered it to be a fairly harmless superstition and any actual punishment was light. Kramer felt the danger from witches must be taken more seriously, and so he responded with this manual on witch hunting.

The first part outlines why witchcraft is a real and persistent danger, citing philosophers and church fathers from Aristotle to St. Augustine to St. Thomas Aquinas. The second part deals with the methods and effects of witchcraft, and how to counter those effects. The third part gives procedures for the accusation and trial of witches, how torture may be used to exact confessions, and finally how to pronounce and execute sentences against the guilty. The text varies between the finer points of theology and canon law, and sensational descriptions of sexual liaisons with devils.

Kramer’s reasoning is extensively based on church canon law and Catholic theology, but his views were not shared by much of the church, and he even faced some opposition. He did, however, secure a papal bull from Innocent VIII approving of his work. Kramer also includes a “letter of approbation” from university faculty who supposedly endorsed his work, though this is thought to be forged.

This translation, published in 1928, includes a lengthy introduction by Montague Summers, who seems sympathetic to the text. He added copious footnotes that give some context to the ancient and medieval references. Also included is the papal bull, and a bibliography of this book’s publishing history.

items.title: The Fall of Robespierre
items.author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Robert Southey
items.content:
The French revolutionary Maximilien Robespierre has risen to prominence within the new French National Convention. A radical Jacobin, he oversees the draconian planning and implementation of the Reign of Terror, including mass arrests and summary executions. But as his policies result in more and more bloodshed, he begins to fear that a conspiracy is afoot—one that will eventually turn the Convention, and the very policies he champions, against him.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge and Robert Southey wrote this poetic drama less than three months after Robespierre was guillotined in the Place de la Révolution. Originally Coleridge was to write the first act, Southey the second, and Robert Lovell the third; but Southey was displeased with Lovell’s contribution, so Southey rewrote it himself.

items.title: The Wheels of Chance
items.author: H. G. Wells
items.content:
is one of H. G. Wells’ comic novels, published in 1896. It satirizes the era’s craze for cycling in Britain, soon after bicycles became easily available and affordable, and before the rise of the automobile.

The novel features the experiences of a humble draper’s assistant, Mr. Hoopdriver, who buys a second-hand bicycle and sets off on a touring holiday. Partway through his trip he encounters an attractive young woman dressed in cycling gear: that is, with pants rather than a skirt. When it appears that the young lady is in trouble, Hoopdriver comes to the rescue, and a series of amusing incidents ensue. As part of its comedy, the book makes some sharp observations about British class structure.

was published shortly after Wells’ first venture into science fiction with . Because they were both short works, some early editions paired the two books into one volume.

items.title: The Mummy!
items.author: Jane C. Loudon
items.content:
In the twenty-second century, under a government headed by female sovereigns, England finds itself in an age of relative tranquility after three centuries of political volatility. Edric Montagu, the younger son of a baronet, finds himself the subject of a scheme to arrange his marriage to the niece of the Duke of Cornwall—a scheme in which he wants no part. Disillusioned and restless, Edric finds himself enticed by the strange theories proposed by Dr. Entwerfen, a scientist who believes that by using the power of electricity, it may be possible to reanimate a sufficiently well-preserved corpse. Defying his father, Edric sets off for Egypt to engage in a bold experiment to revive the mummy of King Cheops, utterly ignorant of exactly what he’s about to awaken—or the profound fate that it will soon unleash upon the English empire.

The Mummy! A Tale of the Twenty-Second Century was first published in 1827, with a second edition published in 1828 that made substantial changes. Jane C. Loudon, orphaned at age seventeen, wrote it as a means to an income. It was published anonymously, only later being publicly attributed to her.

is the first work of science fiction to feature a resurrected mummy. It was written in an era defined by Egyptomania spurred by Napoleon’s recent invasion of Egypt. The future society that Loudon imagines juxtaposes traditional 19th century British society with various technological advances, some conceptually familiar to a 21st century reader, and others both ambitious and fantastical. The modern reader will still find some of Louden’s imagined advancements remarkably forward-looking, like criminal trials argued by automaton lawyers that can speak every language, painting a picture of a future that still feels like science fiction two centuries later.
